title: The framework decompresses content types on your behalf, so the decoder is attack surface even where your code never mentions it
index_line: T-0041 · MEM_WRITE · automatic content-encoding decode puts a native decoder in every request path · c/any-runtime-with-zlib · corroborated
invariant_violated: Attack surface is assumed to be the code that parses *your* protocol. But the runtime decompresses content encodings and the HTTP client/decompress middleware inflates bodies automatically — so a native decoder written in C is in the path of every request and response, and its output buffer sizing depends on length fields inside the compressed stream, which are attacker data.

mechanism.does: an attacker supplies a compressed body (or hosts a response) whose format-level length fields disagree with the actual data
the runtime's HTTP layer or client library recognises the content-encoding and hands the bytes to the decoder without the application asking
the decoder computes an output extent from metadata inside the stream and, on the malformed path, fails to enforce it
the copy writes past the end of the destination buffer
adjacent heap structures are corrupted into control flow the attacker can steer

source.http.body.value: a request or response body with a content-encoding header — the application never sees it; the transport does the parsing

sink.memory.copy.value: the decoder's copy/allocation loop, sized from stream metadata

size.length.value: the format's own length/count fields, which the encoder never has to be honest about

guard.none.value: the application has no decoder-level validation and cannot add any — the bug is below its API

preconditions.expr: the runtime or an HTTP client auto-decompresses the encoding in question

check.spec: node -e "const z=require('zlib');console.log(typeof z.brotliDecompress)"; python3 -c "import brotli" 2>/dev/null && echo brotli-present

preconditions.expr: the decoder build predates the fixed release
the attacker controls a body that reaches the decoder (an upload, a proxied response, a server-side fetch)

success: a crash or memory corruption from a body the application never parsed — the stack is inside the decompressor
the same payload is inert when the content-encoding header is removed, and reaches the decoder when it is present
the corrupted allocation appears in a heap dump next to decoder-internal structures
failure_like: the decoder detects the invalid stream and stops before writing (the fix: validate before extending the output)
false_positive: a decompression *error* page — malformed input rejected cleanly is the safe behaviour
a crash in application code that happens to run after decompression; the stack must be inside the decoder

hazards: inventory the decoders, not the code: image codecs (including WASM builds), compression, character sets, and archive formats are all in this class and all sit below the app's API
an SSE/ASGI/servlet middleware or an HTTP client's `Accept-Encoding` can put the decoder in the path even when the handler never mentions compression
the fix is input validation inside the decoder — no application-level filter can substitute for it
WASM builds (in-browser image decoders, `sharp`-style native modules) have the same bugs with a different exploitability profile
non_transfers: builds using a pure-managed decoder with bounds checks
deployments that strip content-encoding and refuse compressed bodies

evidence.target: Brotli decoder 1.0.3–1.2.0 as shipped in Node.js (CVE-2026-111497, 'node2shell'/'broccoli2shell')
